extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, university press officers, science journalists, and science-interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidence about accuracy and exaggeration in academic press releases for health/biomedical research, and recommendations to improve accountability and transparency in press communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving direct advice to readers to change their behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three common types of exaggeration the study focused on: "giving direct advice to readers to change their behaviour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid issuing press releases that go beyond the paper by telling readers to change behaviour unless the paper itself supports such advice. The study found 40% of press releases contained exaggerated advice and when press releases contained such exaggeration, news was more likely to too (58%); when press releases did not contain exaggeration, news rates were much lower (17%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Making causal claims from correlational (observational) data
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the three common types of exaggeration: "making causal claims from correlational (observational) data."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present correlational findings as causal relationships in press releases. The study found 33% of press releases contained exaggerated causal claims; presence of such exaggeration in press releases was strongly associated with exaggeration in news (81%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Making inference about humans from animal findings
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the three common types of exaggeration: "making inference about humans from animal findings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overgeneralising animal-study results to humans in press releases unless the original research provides appropriate support. The study found 36% of press releases made such inferences; when present in press releases, news exaggeration rates were high (86%), while absence in press releases was associated with much lower news exaggeration (10%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare press releases with the associated peer-reviewed paper and news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate press-release accuracy by analysing press releases alongside their associated peer reviewed research papers and news stories (the method used in the study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically compare wording and claims in the press release to the primary research paper to identify exaggeration; then check whether similar exaggerations appear in subsequent news coverage to assess the source of distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat academic press releases as part of the scientific publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should be treated as a part of the scientific publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt publication-like standards for press releases (transparency, traceability, and peer visibility) so they are subject to similar norms and scrutiny as formal scientific outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include named individuals from the original research paper in press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases "should include named individuals from the original research paper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming authors/building direct links to the research team increases accountability and enables verification by peers and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link press releases to the paper they are promoting
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should be "linked to the paper they are promoting."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide direct links to the full paper so readers and journalists can check primary sources and context, reducing the chance of misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present press releases as online data appendices, in full view of peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should be "presented as online data appendices, in full view of peers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archiving press releases alongside published papers creates an information trail and makes press communications part of the scholarly record available for scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunity for feedback in the publishing journal
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be "opportunity for feedback in the publishing journal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing peer and public feedback on press releases (via journal platforms or linked mechanisms) helps correct inaccuracies and promotes accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic and author accountability for press-release content
rubrics_metrics.description: Academics "should be made accountable for exaggerations in press releases about their own work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that researchers share responsibility for how their findings are communicated (e.g., sign-off on press texts, co-publishing press material) to reduce misleading claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an information trail and public accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies to create an "information trail, and accountability among peers and the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine naming, linking, archiving, and feedback mechanisms so press releases can be audited and actors held accountable for misleading statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider public ranking of press releases to change academic behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculation that a public ranking of press releases "might change academic behaviour, and create an environment where researchers finally act to prevent patients and the public being routinely misled."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incentives/disincentives (e.g., public evaluations or rankings) to reward accurate press communications and discourage sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-promotional and sensationalist framing driven by institutional competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors note the blame lies with "the increasing culture of university competition and self promotion, interacting with the increasing pressures on journalists to do more with less time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press offices and researchers should resist promotional language and sensationalist framing motivated by competitive incentives; prioritize accurate representation of study limitations and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prioritize news uptake over accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: There was "little evidence that exaggeration in press releases increased the uptake of news."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because exaggeration does not clearly boost media coverage, press offices should not sacrifice accuracy in hopes of greater news uptake.
